title: Service Mesh
description: Understand how service meshes like Istio and Linkerd move networking concerns out of application code into infrastructure, enabling mTLS, traffic shifting, and observability at scale.

segments.text: Every microservice needs retries, timeouts, circuit breakers, mutual TLS, and metrics. When you have two hundred services, implementing this in each one is insanity. Service meshes extract all networking logic into a sidecar proxy that runs alongside every service.

Envoy is the workhorse proxy. Originally built at Lyft, it handles every byte of traffic between services. It's a Layer seven proxy — meaning it understands HTTP, gRPC, and can make routing decisions based on headers, paths, even request bodies.

The data plane is all the Envoy sidecars collectively. Every service-to-service call goes through two proxies — the calling service's sidecar and the receiving service's sidecar. This is where mTLS happens. Certificates rotate automatically, zero application code changes needed.

Istio's control plane — specifically istiod — pushes configuration to all Envoy sidecars. It handles certificate authority duties, service discovery, and translates high-level routing rules into Envoy configuration. One control plane managing thousands of proxies.

Traffic shifting is where the mesh shines. Want to canary a new version? Route one percent of traffic to v2, monitor error rates, then gradually increase. No load balancer changes, no DNS tricks. Just a VirtualService config: weight ninety-nine to v1, weight one to v2.

Because every request passes through Envoy, you get distributed tracing for free. Each sidecar injects trace headers — B3 or W3C Trace Context — and reports spans. You see the full request path across fifty services without adding a single line of instrumentation code.
Here's the critical question for your design interviews. A service mesh adds latency to every single request — two extra network hops. When would this cost outweigh the benefits?
segments.thought_prompt: In what scenarios would the latency overhead of a service mesh be unacceptable?

segments.text: Envoy adds roughly one to three milliseconds per hop. For a request that chains through ten services, that's twenty to sixty extra milliseconds. High-frequency trading? Unacceptable. Typical web apps? Totally fine. Uber runs Envoy on their most latency-sensitive paths and optimizes with connection pooling.

Linkerd versus Istio is a real architectural decision. Linkerd is simpler — written in Rust, lower resource footprint, easier to operate. Istio is more powerful — richer traffic management, but significantly more complex. Linkerd uses about ten megabytes of memory per proxy. Istio's Envoy uses fifty to one hundred megabytes.
If you're running a thousand pods, that memory difference matters enormously. A thousand Envoy sidecars at one hundred megabytes each is a hundred gigabytes of memory just for proxies.
segments.thought_prompt: How would you justify the resource cost of a service mesh to your VP of Engineering?

segments.text: The killer feature is zero-trust networking via mTLS. Every service proves its identity with a certificate on every request. No more trusting the network perimeter. When Capital One had their breach in 2019, services inside the perimeter were wide open. mTLS would have contained the blast radius significantly.

Service meshes are infrastructure for service-to-service communication. Use them when you have more than twenty services and need consistent security, observability, and traffic management. The operational overhead is real — plan for a dedicated platform team. Next, we tackle service discovery — how services actually find each other.
